## Recovery Indicators Continue to be Mixed 



- We have made some minor revisions to our estimates for 2009 and we now believe that global copper wirerod consumption fell by 7.6% to 12.9 million tonnes. Whilst the fall in consumption in North America and Europe was around 23%, North East Asia recorded a more modest 13.1% decline and the Rest of the World posted a rise of 4.3% on the back of strong growth in China. China’s share of global copper wire and cable production increased by over six percentage points to 38.0%. 



- This means that for North America, Europe and North East Asia copper wirerod and wire and cable production in 2009 was at its lowest level for at least a decade, but for the Rest of the World it was at a new peak with copper wire and cable production in this grouping accounting for 59% of the global total. However, the leading global cable companies are all still based in the USA, Western Europe, Japan or South Korea. 



- Despite the fact that at a global level the recovery is underway there are still mixed messages coming out of most markets. Even in China there are some concerns about how strong 2010 will be, and in other countries it often seems to be a case of two steps forward and one back. This indicates that the recovery remains quite fragile and there is still a risk that it could be derailed by an as yet unforeseen economic shock.

Page 3 of 12 © 2010 CRU International Ltd **confidential** March 2010 Copper wire, cable and wirerod **www.crugroup.com** # Europe ### **Copper wirerod developments** Since our last monitor in January, we have revised up our estimates for copper wirerod production in Europe to 636,000 tonnes in Q4 2009, with stronger than expected output in Italy. That was a 15.9% year-on-year decline. Copper wirerod production for the full 2009 is estimated to have reached 2,750,000 tonnes, a 20.7% contraction from the previous year. Western European copper wirerod output accounted for 48% of all copper and alloy semi-fabricated products in 2008. However, 2009 was a particularly challenging year with a lot of industry restructuring in Europe. Now that the **Chauny** copper wirerod plant in **France** has stopped operations, we anticipate that there is some 70,000 – 100,000 tonnes of external business for others to pick up. Before closing the plant, **Nexans** agreed with **Aurubis** to supply wirerod for the duration of a strike that took place. Therefore, we expect that Aurubis, **La Farga** , **Cunext** and some **Italian** fabricators will continue to pick up some market share. The **Lens** facility will continue operations; however, industry participants reported that the plant is in need of maintenance; this may disrupt production in the future. Our estimated trade numbers show that **German** exports of copper wirerod in Q4 2009 were up by 2.5% y-o-y to 91,000 tonnes, but for the whole of 2009, German copper wirerod exports saw a 25.6% fall to 365,000 tonnes. Even though market sentiment was far less uncertain at the end of 2009 compared with the previous year, market participants were reluctant to build stock due to soaring copper prices. ### **The copper wire and cable sector** European copper wire and cable production is estimated to have amounted to 2,153,000 tonnes in 2009, a 23.4% decline from 2008. Production in Q4 was an estimated 493,000 tonnes, down by 17% from the same period of the previous year. This figure in Q4 2009 sounds less severe than the Q1, Q2, and Q3 contraction (27%, 26% and 22% respectively). However, it should be seen with caution as it is compared against Q4 2008, which was already impacted by the economic slowdown. The product segment that realised the steepest decline in 2009 was winding wire; production reached an estimated 371,000 tonnes, down by 31.0% from 2008. The drop in the annual copper wire and cable production is consistent with the 2009 sales figures announced by major European players. **Draka** reported that sales volumes in 2009 fell by 18%. Also, **Nexans** said that its cable business experienced an organic shrinkage of 17.2%. ### **Country focus: Russia** According to industry sources, copper wir

|able only|||||||||||| |Data: CRU||||||||||||| © 2010 CRU International Ltd **confidential** Page 5 of 12 March 2010 Copper wire, cable and wirerod **www.crugroup.com** # North America ### **Revised data: NA wire and cable market fell by 23.5% y-o-y in 2009** We have updated the numbers for 2009, which now show that the North American cable industry experienced a slightly smaller decline compared to our previous estimates. North American copper wirerod output shrank by 22.4% in 2009 compared to the previous year, with most of the decline coming from the USA, whereas wirerod consumption dropped 23.1% y-o-y. This indicates that rod producers might be keeping a slightly higher level of stocks, but downstream demand is still sluggish. Copper cable production in North America declined by 23.0% in 2009, with winding wire output being the hardest hit. The copper wire and cable market in the region was down 23.5% y-o-y to 1.4 million tonnes conductor in 2009. As a result of the continuing weakness especially in the automotive, construction and appliances sectors, all the three wire and cable segments showed a significant y-o-y decline, with winding wire showing the largest decline from prior year at 30.5%, and the energy cable segment showing a 23.4% y-oy decline. The communication cable segment was down by 17.3% from the prior year. ### **The construction market is nowhere near full recovery** New privately owned housing starts in January 2010 were up 21.1% y-o-y and up 2.8% from the previous month to a seasonally adjusted annual rate of 5

91,000, the highest since November 2008, according to the Census Bureau. On the other hand, housing completions in January fell by 12.4% m-o-m and 15.3% y-oy to a seasonally adjusted annual rate of 659,000. Home sales also dropped to a record low in January. Since the housing market was in deep recession in early 2009, the double digit percentage growth in housing starts only means that the market is stabilising but does not signal a significant improvement. It will also take time for the increase to show in cable consumption due to the lag between construction starts and when wires and cables are installed. Commercial construction is unlikely to show any upturn before 2011. Market participants said that overall construction activities seemed to be consistent in January 2010 and there is scope for better demand at the earliest in the second half of this year. As for power utility products, consumption was impacted by project delays and low usage by the industrial base. ### **Automotive production takes the lead in North America** The winding wire sector saw consumption plummet in Q4 2009 by 27% y-o-y to 43,000 tonnes conductor, the lowest since our database began in 1998. The automotive sector’s performance lately is in line with the belief that the market has reached bottom. Total US vehicle production in January 2010 was 576,349 units, compared to 283,417 units for the same month in 2009, according to Ward’s Auto. Canadian auto production also increased y-o-y significantly by 75,630 units to 142,497 units while Mexican output rose in the same month by 102% y-o-y to 171,331 units. Downstream auto retailers in North America are restocking recently as a result of recuperating sales. We also understand that Canadian auto purchases, especially in resource-rich Alberta and British Columbia, are particularly supported by revenues from the strong energy markets and the Winter Olympics. The improvements should feed into the winding wire production but to what extent these are sustainable is another matter, with the unemployment rate persisting at high levels in the whole region. © 2010 CRU International Ltd **confidential** Page 7 of 12 March 2010 Copper wire, cable and wirerod **www.crugroup.com** # North East Asia ### **Japanese recovery momentum continued into Q4 2009** According to data released by the **Japanese Electric Makers’ Association** , copper wire and cable shipments rose by 2.5% y-o-y to 54,000 tonnes in January 2010. The figure was down by 3.4% from 55,926 tonnes in December 2009. Sales in January saw the first y-o-y increase since September 2008. However, this growth should be seen with caution as shipments in January 2009 were severely hit by the economic recession. If January 2010 shipments are compared with January 2008, before the economic slowdown impacted the market, the figure is still down by 20%. Our numbers show that copper wirerod production in Japan totalled 667,000 tonnes in 2009, a 20.3% y-o-y contraction. Output in Q4 was down by 7% y-o-y; however, it exhibited 11% sequential recovery from Q3, indicating that the reco

very trend that started in Q2 was sustained until the end of 2009. We have estimated that copper cable shipments amounted to 596,000 tonnes in 2009, a contraction of 19.5% y-o-y. The figure in Q4 2009 totalled 158,600 tonnes; that was up by 4.4% from the previous quarter, providing some further recovery evidence. However, shipments were still down by 11.9% compared to the same period of 2008. ### **Slower South Korean exports to China in Q4 impacted wirerod production** Copper wirerod production in South Korea reached 680,000 tonnes in 2009, consistent with our earlier estimates in January. The figure was up from the previous year by 8.5%. We have revised production in Q4 slightly down from our earlier estimates to 156,000 tonnes, and although output was up by 9.5% from Q4 2008, it suffered a 9.4% sequential shrinkage. The annual increase in South Korean wirerod production was driven by higher exports to China. Until 2008, South Korean wirerod exports were in long-term decline, primarily explained by the establishment of new capacity in China. However, exports to China in 2009 soared to 90,000 tonnes, an increase of 43%. This is partly explained by a tighter scrap market in 2009 and also the strength of the Chinese market. Export volumes were particularly strong in Q2 and Q3 but contracted sequentially in Q4, which is also reflected in the wirerod production volume. Domestic copper wirerod consumption in wire and cable amounted to 452,000 tonnes in 2009, a 0.7% decline from 2008. ### **Taiwanese wire and cable production recovery decelerates in Q4** Further to new data releases, we have revised our copper wirerod figures for Taiwan. Production in 2009 totalled 362,000 tonnes; that was a 14.6% drop from the previous year. The figure in Q4 was 106,000 tonnes. Compared with the same period in 2008 this represented a 25.7% increase; however, output in Q4 2008 had contracted by 24% q-o-q, as the recession hit. Copper wirerod production in Q4 2009 was still down by 2% from Q4 2007. Copper wirerod used in wire and cable amounted to 274,000 tonnes in 2009, down by 16.5% from 2008. The figure declined sequentially by 5.4% in Q4, after strong, doubledigit q-o-q growth realised in Q2 and Q3. Production of power cable reached 230,000 tonnes in 2009, a decline of 14.1% from the previous year. Output in Q4 2009 rose by 5.6% y-o-y to 59,000 tonnes, but from a q-o-q point of view, power cable production dropped by 8.9%. Chinese copper wire and cable production growth of 11.7% helped limit the global decline to 7.7%. Excluding China global copper wire and cable production fell by 16.6%, and as a result China’s share of global copper wire and cable production increased from 31.4% in 2008 to 38.0% in 2009. To put this in context the next largest country, the USA, accounted for just 8.3% of the world total. With China accounting for such a large share of the global cable industry it will clearly be by far the main factor in determining how 2010 looks. It is always

difficult to gauge the outlook for the Chinese market based on the first couple of months of the year, due to the impact of the Chinese New Year celebrations, but our initial feedback from the market is that there is some concern that the recent strong growth can be maintained in 2010. This is particularly true in the power cable sector where the announcement that the Chinese State Grid is to cut investment by a quarter in 2010 is causing worries. Without more details it is difficult to fully assess the impact of this on copper cable demand since most of the transmission grid uses aluminium overhead lines. However, it seems likely that it will have some impact and we have calculated that up to a maximum of around 80,000 tonnes of copper conductor could be at risk. 

For many power cable manufacturers 2010 has started slowly with bad weather in Northern China hitting the construction sector. Also the rising price of copper is leading to cautious buying amongst many users. For copper telecom manufacturers the prospect is for further falls in the market this year as fibre optic cables continue to grow their share. This sector has been shrinking at over 20% a year for the last two years and this is expected to continue. On a more positive note winding wire manufacturers remain optimistic that the market will pick up in March and April as both home and export demand for appliances grows, but again the high price of copper may slightly dampen demand.  Economic indicators remain strongly positive with power consumption up 40% year-on-year in January and car sales up 113%, although these numbers are boosted by comparisons with a weak January 2009. This has led to the government applying further calming measures with lending falling 14% year-on-year in January and the base rate being raised by 0.5%. Further tightening of monetary policy is possible and the impact of stimulus packages is likely to wane in 2010. 

### **Brazilian market drops in 2009, but recovery is underway** 

Based on some new data we now estimate that Brazilian copper cable production fell by 8.6% in 2009 to 236,000 tonnes conductor. The hardest hit sector was winding wire where output fell by an estimated 14.6%. Despite this fall winding wire is still a very important part of the Brazilian cable industry, with 35% of all copper used in wire and cable production consumed in this sector in 2009. The construction and manufacturing sectors both began to recover in H2 2009 after a weak H1, and a range of indicators point to the fact that Brazil is already on the path to recovery. This gives cause for optimism about the outlook for 2010 and beyond, with the market soon to be further boosted by preparations for the 2014 football World Cup and 2016 Olympics.
